9854:
The Reformers rejected the medieval view in which justification depended on infused righteousness and progress in holiness; they made justification a completed verdict and sanctification its necessary fruit. Westminster chapter 13 (1647) codified the view, and Puritans wrote extensively on the practice of holiness.

In the nineteenth century the Reformed view was sharpened against Wesleyan perfectionism and Keswick teaching. Ryle, Charles Hodge and above all B. B. Warfield argued that these movements promised what scripture does not, and that sin remains in believers until glorification. In the twentieth century John Murray introduced the notion of definitive sanctification, and the view was presented in the multi-view books of 1987 (Anthony Hoekema) and 1988 (Ferguson).

John Wesley taught that, beyond the new birth, God offers believers in this life a further work of grace: entire sanctification or Christian perfection, in which the heart is cleansed from inbred sin and filled with perfect love for God and neighbor. It is received by faith, often instantaneously, though preceded and followed by gradual growth. Wesley defined it carefully: not freedom from ignorance, mistakes, infirmities or temptation, and not absolute perfection, but freedom from voluntary transgression of known law and a heart governed by love. It can be lost, and it is never a resting place.

In the nineteenth century, Phoebe Palmer's 'altar theology' taught that if a believer places all on the altar (Christ), the altar sanctifies the gift, so one may claim entire sanctification by faith immediately on the basis of God's promise and testify to it. This 'shorter way' fueled the Holiness movement, its camp meetings, and churches such as the Church of the Nazarene, the Wesleyan Church and the Salvation Army.

Wesley's doctrine emerged from the Oxford Holy Club, his reading of Thomas à Kempis, Jeremy Taylor, William Law and Eastern fathers, and the Methodist revival from 1738. He urged Methodists to 'go on to perfection' and gathered testimonies of those who claimed it.

American Methodism in the early nineteenth century saw the doctrine decline, and Phoebe Palmer and others revived it. After the Civil War, the National Camp Meeting Association for the Promotion of Holiness (1867) spread it widely; tensions with Methodist leadership led to new Holiness denominations around 1880–1910. Holiness preachers increasingly used Pentecostal language ('baptism with the Holy Ghost') for entire sanctification, setting the stage for Pentecostalism.

9967:
Keswick theology, named after the annual convention begun in 1875 in Keswick, England, teaches that many Christians live defeated lives because they try to be holy by their own effort. The remedy is a crisis of full surrender (consecration) followed by a continuous life of faith in which believers 'let go and let God': they reckon themselves dead to sin and rest in Christ, who lives his life through them. The sinful nature is not eradicated, as Wesleyans claimed, but it is continually counteracted by the indwelling Spirit, so that consistent victory over known sin is possible.

Hannah Whitall Smith's *The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life* (1875) popularized the message with images of the believer as clay in the potter's hands and of resting in God's keeping. Keswick distinguishes 'carnal' and 'spiritual' Christians and expects a deeper, Spirit-filled life marked by peace, power and missionary zeal. It was enormously influential in evangelical missions and devotional writing through much of the twentieth century.
9970: Boardman's *The Higher Christian Life* adapted Holiness teaching for non-Methodists, describing a second experience of full trust in Christ for sanctification, and he later worked with the Smiths in British conferences.

9983:
The Higher Life movement grew out of American Holiness revivalism but was adapted to Anglican, Presbyterian and Quaker contexts in Britain, where Wesleyan eradication language was unwelcome. After the Smiths' conferences at Oxford (1874) and Brighton (1875), the Keswick Convention became an annual gathering whose week moved from conviction of sin, to God's provision, to consecration, to Spirit-filling, to service.

Keswick shaped the devotional lives of missionaries (for example Hudson Taylor's 'exchanged life'), writers such as Andrew Murray, F. B. Meyer and later Watchman Nee, and American institutions such as Moody Bible Institute and Dallas Theological Seminary. Critics including J. C. Ryle, B. B. Warfield and later J. I. Packer and Andrew Naselli argued that its teaching was unbiblical and pastorally harmful. The Keswick Convention itself moved toward a broader expository evangelicalism in the later twentieth century.
